name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of having a language model answer legal questions only from documents that have first been fetched and placed in front of it, rather than from whatever the model absorbed during training. The retrieved set is usually a defined corpus: statutes, regulations, reported decisions, contracts, internal memos, or a matter-specific collection assembled for one engagement. The point is that every assertion in the output can be traced back to a passage the researcher can open and read. It sits inside legal research and case strategy as the evidence layer, the part that decides which authorities are even in play before any argument is drafted.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of having a language model answer legal questions only from documents that have first been fetched and placed in front of it, rather than from whatever the model absorbed during training. The retrieved set is usually a defined corpus: statutes, regulations, reported decisions, contracts, internal memos, or a matter-specific collection assembled for one engagement. The point is that every assertion in the output can be traced back to a passage the researcher can open and read. It sits inside legal research and case strategy as the evidence layer, the part that decides which authorities are even in play before any argument is drafted.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system runs on a document store plus a search index, with an embedding model for semantic matching and a keyword index such as BM25 for exact terms, citations and defined phrases. A retrieval layer queries both and merges the results, often with a reranker that reorders candidate passages by relevance to the question. The language model then reads only the passages passed to it and produces an answer with citations pointing at those passages. Everything sits behind access controls, because the corpus may contain privileged material, client confidences or licensed database content that cannot leave the firm's environment.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts by defining the corpus and the question narrowly enough that retrieval can succeed, since a vague query returns vague authority. The researcher runs the query, inspects the retrieved passages, and discards anything off point before generation, because a model given weak passages will still write confidently around them. The draft answer is then checked citation by citation against the source text, and any proposition without a supporting passage is treated as unsupported. Good practice includes testing the pipeline on questions with known answers, watching for retrieval that misses a controlling authority, and keeping a record of which corpus version produced which answer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The central risk is a citation that looks correct and is not, whether because the model paraphrased beyond the passage or because the retrieved authority was superseded or never good law. Privilege and confidentiality rules still apply to whatever enters the corpus, and licensed research databases carry contractual limits on storage and reuse. Professional conduct duties around competence, supervision and candour mean a lawyer remains responsible for the filing even when a tool drafted it. Provenance is the control: each answer should carry the passages it relied on, the corpus and version searched, and the date, so the work can be reproduced and defended later.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect retrieval to move closer to the primary sources themselves, with citators and official repositories feeding the index so that currency and treatment are checked inside the pipeline rather than after it. Evaluation is shifting from whether an answer reads well to whether its citations hold up under inspection, which pushes teams toward measurable grounding rather than fluent prose. Courts are beginning to require disclosure when generative tools contributed to a filing, and that pressure will shape how these systems log their work. The durable division of labour is likely to stay the same: retrieval and drafting get faster, and the lawyer still reads the authority before signing.
